comparator.name: Sociology
comparator.route: Social Networks year-two field and project; Labour Sociology year-three field course
comparator.sourceNotes: The current programme-specific regulations account for the full 180 EC: 60 EC compulsory in year one; 45 EC fixed sociology and methods, one 5-EC field course and its corresponding 10-EC project in year two; and a 30-EC broadening minor, 25 EC fixed work and one different 5-EC field course in year three. The normalized registry target names the general bachelor and supplies no student-specific field preference. The route therefore uses the first listed year-two field course (Social Networks), its required corresponding project, and then the first listed year-three field course not already taken (Labour Sociology), before considering UCR fit. The 30-EC broadening minor remains genuine approved choice space. The official current bachelor page independently confirms the 180-EC duration, field-specialisation structure and live curriculum.

routeSelection.route: Social Networks year-two field and project; Labour Sociology year-three field course
routeSelection.basis: The generic target does not name one of the four field specialisations. The formal 2026–2027 regulations list Social Networks first for the year-two choose-one set and require the project to correspond, so Social Networks and Project Social Networks are selected. Year three requires one field course not already taken; Labour Sociology is the first remaining item in the same official list. This neutral source-order decision was made before assessing UCR fit.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Sociological theory about institutions, relationships, norms, inequality and social change
Qualitative and quantitative social research, statistics, data collection and evidence-based analysis
Social welfare, education, work, health and unequal life chances
Applied projects, policy research, professional development and an independent sociology thesis
adjacent: Work, organisations, markets, public institutions and organisational inequality
Crime, public safety, cybercrime, law and institutional responses
Social networks, media, collective behaviour, health and ageing
questions: How do social institutions and relationships create or reduce public problems and inequality?
How can mixed social evidence be translated into policy and practical solutions?
How do digital media, neighbourhoods and collective behaviour shape social values and safety?

alternatives.label: Sociology, inequality & social research
alternatives.concept: A broad sociology-led programme combining the complete available UCR sociology sequence with mixed social research, inequality, institutions, political economy, public health, media and policy.
alternatives.labelReason: Five dedicated Sociology courses and a substantial qualitative, statistical and data-analysis spine anchor the schedule; its supporting courses consistently address inequality, institutions, public problems and social change.
progression: Introductory sociology, institutions, research and statistics precede modern theory, inequality, qualitative and quantitative analysis, public health, global relations and advanced social research. All prerequisites and planned offerings pass; seven level-3 courses are included.

alternatives.label: Work, organisations & social inequality
alternatives.concept: A sociology programme focused on how labour markets, organisations, leadership, public policy and economic institutions produce or reduce inequality, supported by qualitative and quantitative research.
alternatives.labelReason: The complete UCR sociology sequence is reinforced by organisational psychology, leadership and diversity management, negotiation, economics, public economics and econometrics, making work and organisational inequality the schedule’s visible secondary centre.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the closest programme, this direction replaces eight courses in public health, media, international institutions and broader data work with organisational psychology, leadership, negotiation, public economics and economic history; its academic centre is work and organisations rather than general public problems.
progression: Research Methods & Statistics precedes the leadership, public-economics and econometrics courses that require it; gateway psychology precedes Lifespan Developmental Psychology. Introductory sociology and social science precede advanced organisational, economic and sociological work, and all planned offerings pass.

alternatives.label: Crime, public safety & digital society
alternatives.concept: A sociological study of crime, offending, public safety, law and institutional responses, with psychology, media and data analysis supporting attention to cybercrime and digitally mediated social risks.
alternatives.labelReason: Sociology and mixed methods remain the foundation, while five law courses, justice, political institutions, forensic psychology, youth extremism, media and data science create a clear crime, safety and digital-society emphasis.
alternatives.distinctness: This direction differs from both prior schedules by at least nine courses and replaces their work, health and general-policy breadth with criminal law, international and human-rights law, forensic psychology, youth extremism and public-safety institutions.
progression: Introductory law, sociology, politics and psychology precede criminal law, quantitative methods, advanced sociology, forensic psychology, international law and systematic evidence review. Formal prerequisites and Fall-2026 cohort offerings pass; eight level-3 courses are included.

selection.assessment: The closest programme provides a broad sociology and mixed-method research spine. Work and organisations, and crime/public safety, are separately generator-eligible directions grounded in the current programme’s named field structure; both yield coherent 24-course schedules, pass feasibility and progression, and differ from each earlier schedule by at least eight courses. Production therefore stops at the three-alternative maximum.

notes.text: Groningen Sociology integrates a full three-year disciplinary sequence, three successive statistics courses plus advanced statistics, two qualitative-methods courses, field-linked commissioned projects and a compulsory bachelor thesis. UCR supports strong interdisciplinary sociology alternatives, but ordinary UCR courses do not reproduce the same continuous project-and-thesis structure or every specialised field course.
The comparator’s 30-EC broadening minor remains open approved choice space. It is not populated with arbitrary Groningen courses or treated as equivalent to fixed UCR selections.
